Where it began

Jason Gillespie was born in Sydney on 19 April 1975 and went to school at Cabra Dominican College in Adelaide. Through his father's side he is a descendant of the Kamilaroi people, and he became the first acknowledged Aboriginal man to play Test cricket for Australia. Faith Thomas had been the first Indigenous Test cricketer of all, back in 1958.

He held a scholarship at the Australian Cricket Academy in 1995, played his state cricket for South Australia, and won his first Test cap in November 1996, at Sydney, against the West Indies.

The player

Gillespie was a right-arm fast bowler, accurate and hard to score from. He played 71 Tests between 1996 and 2006 and took 259 wickets at 26.14, with eight five-wicket hauls and a best of seven for 37. In 2004 the ICC put him in its World XI for both Tests and one-day cricket, and he was also named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year.

His last Test, at Chittagong in April 2006, was one to remember. Sent in as nightwatchman, he batted on and on, added 320 with Michael Hussey and finished on 201 not out, on his 31st birthday. It was his first hundred in first-class cricket and set a world record for a nightwatchman. He took eight wickets in the series as well and was named player of the match and of the series.

What made him special

He was the steady partner in a great attack. With Glenn McGrath at one end and Shane Warne waiting, Gillespie's job was to keep the pressure on, and for years he did it with accuracy and very few loose balls. He rarely ran away with a series on his own, and his best haul in one was 20 wickets, but captains always knew what they would get.

With the bat he averaged 18.74, which makes the double hundred all the more delightful. Two years before it, he and McGrath had put on 114 for the last wicket against New Zealand at Brisbane. Neither man had made a fifty before, in Tests or one-day games, and the dressing room loved every run.

Away from the middle

He also played county cricket for Yorkshire and Glamorgan, and after retiring he became a busy and successful coach. He started in Zimbabwe in 2010, then took charge of Yorkshire, who rose from the second division and won the County Championship in 2014 and 2015. He went on to coach the Adelaide Strikers, Papua New Guinea, Sussex and South Australia.

In 2010 a statue of him, the work of the sculptor Ken Martin, went up at the Adelaide Oval. He is in the South Australian Sport Hall of Fame, and in 2021 Australia Post made him one of its Legends of Cricket.

And finally

Gillespie made just one Test hundred, and it was a double. A nightwatchman's job is to survive until the morning; he simply forgot to stop.
